Integration and test of this EPS stacks several independent hazard types—energized mating errors, ground/flight interface noise, connector wear from repeated builds, and crane/handling moves between facilities—each of which has already destroyed or endangered flight hardware on past missions.

### 1. Energized connector mismate during battery/harness mating

Blind or limited-visibility mating of power connectors can short the bus or battery the instant pins touch, before alignment keys fully engage. On Magellan, a technician mating a battery connector to the wrong harness connector caused an electrical short that destroyed the test battery, the battery harness, the flight harness connector, and ignited the thermal blanket, costing over a week on an already tight schedule. Investigators found the connector design allowed pin contact before full keyway engagement and the mate point lacked direct visual access. Recommendations: mate batteries only in a fully discharged state, dress/tie cables so wrong-connector mating is physically impossible, use connectors where pins contact only after full key engagement, avoid blind-mate locations, and design umbilical/direct-access circuitry to tolerate a direct short without damage.

Check: for every battery and bus connector mated under the thermal blanket or in confined harness runs, confirm discharge state before mate, verify keying/visibility, and confirm GSE umbilical circuits are short-tolerant, per [LLIS 386: Magellan Battery Fire](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/386).

### 2. Ground-to-flight ground-loop noise through the umbilical

Running functional tests through a facility umbilical couples GSE ground to flight ground; AC as well as DC paths can inject transients into sensitive circuits. On Galileo, a capacitive coupling path between flight and GSE grounds produced a 7V transient during power surges (e.g., TWTA turn-on) that intermittently triggered a power-on-reset in the attitude control subsystem, despite extensive investigation. Recommendation: verify AC ground paths are testable in system interface verification tests, and analyze interface circuits for AC coupling between independent ground trees.

Check: given the shunt regulator and remote power switches will see bus transients during umbilical-powered testing, verify AC ground-path behavior explicitly in interface tests rather than relying on DC continuity checks alone, per [LLIS 281: Galileo Attitude Control Power on Reset Problem](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/281).

### 3. Pin damage from repeated harness build-up/rework cycling

Connectors mated and demated repeatedly through rework accumulate bent pins, deformed sockets, and misalignment, sometimes going undetected if processing is skipped. Scout program experience (1960s–70s) found unmated or deformed-contact connectors traced to deviation from normal processing and missed visual checks. Recommendations: minimize connector cycling, visually re-inspect both halves before each mating, verify all connectors are mated before proceeding with test, and favor tapered-socket-entry designs.

Check: track mate/demate counts on EPS connectors through each harness reconfiguration, and require visual re-inspection and mate-verification sign-off before each functional test, per [LLIS 470: Electrical Connectors - Scout Program](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/470).

### 4. Lift/move instability between test facilities

Moving the assembled spacecraft between electrical, mass-properties, acoustic, and TV facilities on tight schedule can outrun proper handling-equipment review. On TOPEX/POSEIDON, a T/V lift fixture proved unstable and the suspended spacecraft rotated 135°, nearly falling, because no stability analysis of the full lifted configuration was done and a planned GSE review had been repeatedly postponed. Recommendations: review all handling GSE before use, perform a full stability analysis of the lifted configuration, and run a precursor dry run with a representative mass simulator.

Check: before each inter-facility move on this schedule-constrained flow, confirm GSE review and lift stability analysis are complete and not skipped for schedule, per [LLIS 1089: TOPEX/POSEIDON Spacecraft Handling Anomaly](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/1089).

This is a research aid drawn from historical records, not a safety review.
